shortlist.raw_text: Linear attention offers an efficient solution for long-sequence modeling via linear complexity and fixed-size recurrent states. Gated DeltaNet-2 (GDN-2) introduces independent channel-wise control over erasure and writing, enhancing state-update expressiveness and in-context retrieval, yet it suffers from training failures during long-context training. We trace these failures to the asymmetry between reading and modification directions during erasure, which yields non-normal erase operators whose directional gains accumulate across tokens, triggering exponential state growth even without new writes. To resolve this, we propose , employing symmetric erasure to ensure non-expansive state propagation and decay-regulated residual writing to preserve writing flexibility. Theoretically, we establish an O(T) upper bound on recurrent state growth while retaining chunkwise parallel computation. Experiments on ~1.6B parameter models show that achieves stable training alongside improved long-context retrieval. Compared to GDN-2, it boosts the 128K average RULER score by 6.80 points in the recurrent setting and average accuracy across nine downstream tasks by 0.62 points in the hybrid setting.

shortlist.raw_text: Computer-using agents are increasingly expected to complete realistic user goals rather than isolated GUI actions. However, existing benchmarks typically isolate web, mobile, or desktop environments, leaving it unclear whether a single generalist agent can execute long-horizon workflows that span multiple operating systems and persistent application states. We introduce OS-Omni, a live cross-platform benchmark and execution environment for evaluating computer-using agents across Windows, Ubuntu, macOS, iOS, Android, and Web environments. OS-Omni is released in versioned waves of 300 tasks each; this paper focuses on the first release, v1, which contains 48 tasks per platform and 12 cross-platform workflows that pair a desktop with an Android phone. OS-Omni provides reproducible initialization, platform-specific adapters, trajectory logging, and executable final-state evaluators, and includes controlled service-backed applications for workflows involving account, cart, budget, calendar, message, and other persistent state. Human studies show that OS-Omni tasks require 67.54 interaction steps, substantially exceeding OSWorld references of 15.0 steps. On v1, the strongest evaluated agent, Claude Opus 5.5, reaches 68.5% average success, trailing the 77.3% human reference by 8.8 points; the gap is uneven across platforms, with frontier models exceeding humans on Linux but trailing them by more than 25 points on iOS and macOS. These results indicate that current agents remain far from platform-robust, long-horizon computer use, especially when success requires sustained state tracking and durable final-state changes.

shortlist.raw_text: Establishing effective scaling laws for medical multimodal large language models (MLLMs) remains a persistent and fundamental challenge. Our systematic evaluation shows that existing medical MLLMs tend to underperform frontier general-purpose MLLMs across a range of medical tasks, while scaling model size primarily improves text capabilities rather than multimodal perception, and enabling reasoning modes fails to close this visual gap. To investigate how medical multimodal intelligence scales in practice, we introduce Sage-Med-Preview, a 35B-parameter medical multimodal model with 3B activated parameters, built by combining stage-specific curation over 322.7 million candidate records with a progressive training curriculum spanning medical pretraining, staged supervised fine-tuning, and adaptive reinforcement learning. Across this curriculum, progressive supervised refinement and adaptive reinforcement learning yield consistent stage-wise gains, substantially advancing both specialized visual understanding and medical language capabilities. Evaluated against 77 competing models across 238 clinical tasks spanning 61 public and 13 private multi-center benchmarks in more than 40 modalities, Sage-Med-Preview achieves an average score of 58.26% on the 31 public multimodal benchmarks. It outperforms the state-of-the-art open-source medical model Hulu-Med-235B-A22B at 50.99% and the general scientific model Intern-S2-Preview at 52.24%, and approaches the advanced proprietary model GPT-6.2-Sol across multiple tasks such as comprehensive multimodal understanding, report generation, and visual grounding. Although substantial challenges remain in complex medical reasoning and multi-step clinical workflows, this report provides empirical evidence, actionable data and training recipes, and a rigorous benchmark toward scalable clinical multimodal intelligence.

shortlist.raw_text: A foundation model for time series is pretrained once and then asked to forecast series it has never seen, so the evidence for it is its score on held-out datasets. Such datasets are scarce, and a few public leaderboards carry most comparisons, yet none of them states how small a difference its datasets can detect. We call that quantity the resolution of a board and introduce Vernier, a tool that computes it from the files a board already publishes. Vernier also reports which entries a board cannot separate from its leader and whether its order changes when unrelated parties submit. GIFT-Eval resolves 6.8 rank places, and its displayed neighbours sit 0.91 apart. The ten places of its top ten hold fewer than two resolvable steps. fev-bench, Chronos Benchmark II and TIME show the same pattern: their resolution is 3.6 to 19 times the gap between neighbours. With each of its 2,554 series as an independent source, BOOM is the one board that resolves its top ten. Below the resolution the order depends on who else submitted: across four boards, rules that rank against the pool reversed 43 top-ten pairs with neither entry rerun, in one update in seven. Boards also do not record how much history a model receives. On 70 configurations, shortening it raised the error of three of four open models, two of them by 15%. We release Vernier, which runs this report with one command on any leaderboard that publishes per-dataset scores: https://github.com/therealram18/vernier

shortlist.summary: Complexity theorist and former OpenAI researcher Scott Aaronson argues that AI's recent math breakthroughs matter far beyond academia. The possible consequences, he writes, range from reshaping the global economy to threatening all life on Earth. He's also "virtually certain" that AI labs are sitting on "one or more bombshells" in cryptography. Title: Nvidia hits pause on chip shipments to Southeast Asia

Text:
Nvidia has told manufacturing partners to pause server shipments to Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Indonesia as the U.S. tightens its push to keep AI chips out of China.

Article text (excerpt):
Nvidia is under pressure to do things differently, and a new WSJ report shows how far that’s going.
According to the Journal, Nvidia has told manufacturing partners, including Dell and Super Micro, to hit pause on server shipments to Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, and Indonesia for an unspecified period as it assesses whether its regional partners are meeting U.S. export requirements.
As for why those countries, Chinese companies have been tapping Nvidia chips remotely from data centers there, a loophole the US Commerce Department closed — reportedly grudgingly — earlier this month. The Journal notes that the think tank Institute for Progress estimates remote data centers like these supply about 24% of China’s AI computing power.

(Found by web search. Some coverage may be older background. Use it for context and explanation, but don't present older events as new, and keep the main story's facts primary.)

Coverage from TechCrunch on MSN: "Nvidia hits pause on chip shipments to Southeast Asia"
Nvidia has told manufacturing partners to pause server shipments to Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Indonesia as the U.S. tightens its push to keep AI chips out of China.

Coverage from TechRepublic: "Nvidia Reportedly Halts AI Server Shipments to 4 Southeast Asian Countries Amid US Export Controls"
Nvidia’s reported AI server shipment halt raises procurement and compliance concerns for businesses navigating tighter US export controls in Southeast Asia.

Coverage from Daily Jang: "Nvidia freezes AI server shipments to Southeast Asia amid new US chip crackdown"
US chip giant Nvidia has instructed its major manufacturing partners to stop shipping artificial intelligence servers to four Southeast Asian countries.
According to reports from the “Financial Times” on November 26, 2026, server makers including Dell and Supermicro have told buyers in Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, and Indonesia that their orders are on hold.
The sudden freeze follows sweeping new export controls from the US Commerce Department that took effect last week. Washington aims to stop Chinese tech firms from bypassing direct US bans by renting computing power or buying restricted AI processors through third-party countries.
Under the strict new guidelines, Southeast Asian cloud providers have a 90-day window to secure special US licenses. To qualify, companies must prove that no restricted Chinese entities are among their end users.
However, regional tech executives report widespread confusion because the government has not yet explained how to apply for the paperwork while the 90-day clock is already ticking.
The pause threatens massive revenue streams and major data center projects across the region. Nvidia generated $104 billion through its Singapore unit in 2025 alone.
Meanwhile, banks have already frozen roughly $500 million in loans for a Singapore cloud project tied to TikTok parent company ByteDance. It remains unclear if Nvidia’s halt is a temporary compliance pause or a long-term block.

Background (Regulation of artificial intelligence in the United States, Wikipedia):
The United States federal government and state governments have developed some regulation of artificial intelligence, including executive orders, federal laws, and state laws. Federal agencies have also developed some sector-specific regulations related to AI.

Background (Cloud computing, Wikipedia):
Cloud computing is defined by the International Organization for Standardization (ISO) as "a paradigm for enabling network access to a scalable and elastic pool of shareable physical or virtual resources with self-service provisioning and administration on demand". It is commonly referred to as "the cloud".

text:
Nvidia just told server makers to freeze AI shipments to four Southeast Asian countries.

The freeze hits Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, and Indonesia while the U.S. closes a cloud loophole.

The target is not physical chip sales.

Chinese tech companies were tapping Nvidia processors remotely from data centers in those four nations.

An estimate from the Institute for Progress shows those remote centers supplied roughly 24% of China’s AI computing power.

Now, Washington requires regional cloud providers to get special U.S. licenses proving no restricted Chinese entities are end users.

The clock is ticking on a 90-day window, but regional executives say the government hasn't explained how to apply.

The financial fallout arrived immediately:
• Banks froze roughly $500 million in loans for a Singapore cloud project linked to ByteDance
• Nvidia generated $104 billion through its Singapore unit in 2025 alone
• Dell and Super Micro put orders on hold across all four countries

Major data center projects across the region are suddenly stuck.

My read: stopping chip shipments to China was step one, but policing distant servers that rent compute power is where export control gets messy.

When renting a server across borders becomes a trade violation, neutral data centers lose their neutrality.

Will your company's cloud provider pass the next compliance audit?

Source: TechCrunch, with reporting from TechCrunch on MSN and TechRepublic
